knowledgePattern: Find the prime-divisor exception at the first unsupported proof line
solution:
Lines I–V are valid: the three possible remainders of n on division by 3 show that one of n−2,n,n+2 is a multiple of 3.

Line VI wrongly treats every multiple of 3 as nonprime. The number 3 itself is prime. The consecutive odd integers 3,5,7 therefore contradict the claimed bound.

The first error is line VI: answer G. For completeness, a run of four consecutive odd integers cannot all be prime: a prime run of three would have to be 3,5,7, and either adjoining odd integer is 1 or 9.

hints.title: Check the exact definition
hints.body: At each claimed implication, test whether an exceptional small allowed integer changes the conclusion.
hints.recap: A statement about divisibility must respect the precise integer definition, including its boundary cases.
hints.pitfall: A divisor shows compositeness only when it is a proper divisor greater than 1.
hints.pause: Find the earliest line whose conclusion does not follow from its premise.
